title: Can you discover all subclasses of a sealed class at runtime (`getPermittedSubclasses()`)?
shortTitle: Can you discover all subclasses of a sealed class at runtime (`getPermittedSubclasses()`)?
keyPoints: `Class.getPermittedSubclasses()` returns an array of `Class` objects for the direct permitted subtypes recorded in the class file.
It returns `null` if the class is not sealed; guard with `Class.isSealed()` first.
The method returns only direct permitted subtypes, not transitive descendants.
For a `non-sealed` branch, the open, unlisted subclasses cannot be enumerated reflectively.
Complete runtime discovery is only possible for hierarchies that are closed all the way down (`final`/`sealed`).
Frameworks use this to auto-register serializers, validators, and test cases for each permitted subtype.
The permitted set is authoritative and trustworthy: it is validated by the JVM at load time.

s1_definition.oneliner: `getPermittedSubclasses()` returns the direct permitted subtypes recorded in the class file at runtime, but only the direct ones, not transitive descendants or open `non-sealed` subclasses.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`Class.getPermittedSubclasses()`** – returns a `Class<?>[]` of the direct permitted subtypes recorded in the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute, added in Java 17.
- **`Class.isSealed()`** – returns `true` if the class is sealed; use it as a guard before calling `getPermittedSubclasses()`.
- **Direct only** – returns only direct permitted subtypes, not grandchildren or deeper descendants.
- **`non-sealed` limitation** – cannot enumerate the open, unlisted subclasses beneath a `non-sealed` branch.
- **Authoritative** – the JVM validates the permitted set at load time, so the reflective view is trustworthy.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps the official closed list of which products may directly be "an Account" filed in head office records. At any time a clerk can pull that exact list and read off the approved direct products. But it only lists the direct products; it does not chase down every sub-variant a product might have, and if one product was stamped "open" for partners, the list cannot name the unknown partner products.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Recursive Permitted Subclass Discovery     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│  Account.class.getPermittedSubclasses()     │
│       │                                     │
│       ├── SavingsAccount (final)            │
│       │   └── LEAF ✓                        │
│       │                                     │
│       └── LoanAccount (sealed)              │
│           │                                 │
│           ├── HomeLoan (final)              │
│           │   └── LEAF ✓                    │
│           │                                 │
│           └── CarLoan (final)               │
│               └── LEAF ✓                    │
│                                             │
│  Result: [SavingsAccount, HomeLoan, CarLoan]│
│                                             │
│  Non-sealed branch:                         │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐           │
│  │ PartnerProduct (non-sealed)  │           │
│  │ └── STOP: open, cannot       │           │
│  │     enumerate subtypes       │           │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`Class.getPermittedSubclasses()`, added in Java 17, returns an array of `Class` objects for the direct permitted subtypes that the compiler recorded in the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute. It returns `null` if the class is not sealed, so you guard with `isSealed()` first. Because the permitted set is validated by the JVM at load time, this reflective view is authoritative.

The key limitation is that it returns only the direct permitted subtypes. If a permitted subtype is itself sealed, you must recurse to discover the full leaf set. In a banking project at National Bank of India, `Account` permits `LoanAccount`, which is itself sealed permitting `HomeLoan` and `CarLoan`. Calling `getPermittedSubclasses()` on `Account` returns only `LoanAccount`, not its leaves, so Rajesh recurses to find all three leaves.

The recursion must stop at a `non-sealed` branch, because its subclasses are open and cannot be enumerated. Complete runtime discovery is only possible for hierarchies that are closed all the way down with `final` and `sealed` types.

The practical payoff is framework auto-registration. A serialization layer can derive Jackson subtype mappings directly from `getPermittedSubclasses()`, so the mapping never drifts out of sync with the sealed `permits` list. When a new product is added, the registration picks it up automatically. This pairs beautifully with compile-time exhaustiveness of switches, giving both automatic framework wiring and compiler-checked application code.

Remember one sentence: `getPermittedSubclasses()` returns the direct permitted subtypes at runtime, but you must recurse for the full leaf set and cannot enumerate beyond a `non-sealed` branch.
